The *TDA User’s Manual* stops at chapter 8, and development did not. The
spatial commands, the file readers for formats that postdate the manual,
and TDA’s online help are all in the program and in none of its
documentation. This is what is there.

## What happens inside

There is no reimplementation. TDA’s C, context-threaded and compiled
into the package, runs unchanged; a wrapper writes the command file TDA
would have been given, hands it over in memory, and reads the answer
back. Every object therefore carries the run it came from.

Box 1One fit, and the run underneath it

``` r
d <- tda_rrdat()
fit <- tda_rate(Surv(TFP, DES) ~ EDU, d)
cat(fit$run$commands, sep = "\n")
```

    rdataframe;
    edef(
        ts = Tstart,
        tf = Tfin,
        org = Org,
        des = Des,
    );
    rate(
        mfmt = 24.16,
        tfmt = 24.16,
        xa (0,1) = EDU,
    ) = 2;

The answer arrives on two channels. The console is what TDA printed –
[`tda_output()`](https://janmarvin.github.io/TDA/reference/tda_estimates.md)
shows all of it, and
[`tda_diagnostics()`](https://janmarvin.github.io/TDA/reference/tda_diagnostics.md)
the lines that are errors, warnings or notes, which TDA otherwise leaves
in the middle of its output for the reader to find. The exports are the
doubles behind the numbers TDA printed: coefficients, covariance
matrices, tables, and a tap on every number the console formatter was
handed. A wrapper takes its numbers from the exports and uses the text
only to find its way around, so
[`coef()`](https://rdrr.io/r/stats/coef.html) holds the double TDA
computed, not a number re-read from a print format.

Box 2Printed, and computed

``` r
grep("EDU", fit$run$output, value = TRUE)
```

    [1] "  5 EDU       3   8  24.16 c5"                                                                                
    [2] "  2  1   0   1  A EDU            0.0150660299026325       0.0211574987658471       0.7120893669601657  0.5236"

``` r
sprintf("%.17g", coef(fit)[["EDU"]])
```

    [1] "0.015066029902632524"

``` r
names(fit$run$exports)
```

     [1] "episodes.table"    "episodes.excluded" "rate.logLik.null"  "ml.vcov"          
     [5] "ml.logLik"         "ml.gradient"       "ml.change.f"       "ml.change.p"      
     [9] "rate.est"          "rate.est.names"    "ml.logLik.pair"    "print.values"     
    [13] "print.labels"     

[`tda_output_audit()`](https://janmarvin.github.io/TDA/reference/tda_output_audit.md)
is the check that this holds: it classifies every line TDA printed as
boilerplate, an echo of the input, a setting, a diagnostic, or a number
that is in the object or in the exports, and reports whatever is none of
those. The package’s tests run it over every example in this manual and
over the 634 command files of TDA’s own regression suite.

Box 3Where every line went

``` r
attr(tda_output_audit(fit), "summary")
```

    cls
          blank boilerplate        echo    settings      stored 
             20          13           9          11          18 

## Spatial data

TDA holds points, lines and polygons in a spatial structure of its own,
and has about twenty commands over it. None of them appears in the
manual.

[`tda_spatial()`](https://janmarvin.github.io/TDA/reference/tda_spatial.md)
builds the structure from a data frame. `type = 1` is points; `type = 3`
groups consecutive rows sharing an `id` into one polygon each.

Box 4A spatial structure, and what is in it

``` r
set.seed(7)
pts <- data.frame(id = 1:12, x = round(runif(12), 3), y = round(runif(12), 3))
s <- tda_spatial(pts)
tda_sd_info(s)
```

    Call: tda_sd_info(s)

    Cases: 12 

     points lines polygons xmin  ymin  xmax  ymax
         12     0        0 0.07 0.009 0.989 0.997

[`tda_sd_voronoi()`](https://janmarvin.github.io/TDA/reference/tda_sd_analyses.md)
is the Voronoi diagram. What `sdvd` writes is itself a spatial data file
– points for the vertices, lines for the edges – so the result plots
with the same machinery the input does.

Box 5The Voronoi diagram of those points

``` r
v <- tda_sd_voronoi(s, opt = 2)
plot(v, xlim = c(-0.2, 1.2), ylim = c(-0.2, 1.2))
```

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

[`tda_sd_select()`](https://janmarvin.github.io/TDA/reference/tda_sd_analyses.md)
keeps what falls inside a rectangle and
[`tda_sd_clip()`](https://janmarvin.github.io/TDA/reference/tda_sd_analyses.md)
cuts to it. Both want the rectangle given; TDA will not guess one.

Box 6Selecting and clipping to a region

``` r
tda_sd_select(s, rec = "0,0,0.5,0.5")$table
```

    8 records, lengths 2-5
    [1]  1 1 1 2 1 
    [2]  0.398 0.096 
    [3]  2 1 1 3 1 
    [4]  0.116 0.453 
    [5]  3 1 1 4 1 
    [6]  0.070 0.085 
    [7]   4  1  1 10  1 
    [8]  0.459 0.295 

``` r
tda_sd_clip(s, c(0, 0, 0.5, 0.5))$table
```

    8 records, lengths 2-5
    [1]  1 1 1 2 1 
    [2]  0.398 0.096 
    [3]  2 1 1 3 1 
    [4]  0.116 0.453 
    [5]  3 1 1 4 1 
    [6]  0.070 0.085

Polygons are the same structure with `type = 3`.
[`tda_sd_data()`](https://janmarvin.github.io/TDA/reference/tda_sd_analyses.md)
gives the vertices back as an ordinary data frame, which is the form
most things in R want.

Box 7Two square polygons

``` r
poly <- data.frame(id = c(1, 1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 2, 2),
                   x  = c(0, 2, 2, 0, 3, 5, 5, 3),
                   y  = c(0, 0, 2, 2, 0, 0, 2, 2))
sp <- tda_spatial(poly, type = 3)
tda_sd_data(sp)$table
```

## Reading a shapefile

[`tda_read_shapefile()`](https://janmarvin.github.io/TDA/reference/tda_read_shapefile.md)
reads geometry and attaches the `.dbf` attribute table as `$attributes`.
The manual documents SPSS and Stata files and nothing else; shapefiles,
E00, DCW, GSHHS, `.dbf` and BIFF `.xls` are all readable and all
undocumented. The file is the North Carolina SIDS shapefile that the sf
package ships, read here by TDA itself; these boxes run when sf is
installed.

Box 8North Carolina counties, read through TDA

``` r
nc <- tda_read_shapefile(system.file("shape/nc.shp", package = "sf"))
tda_sd_info(nc)
```

    Call: tda_sd_info(nc)

    Cases: 108 

     points lines polygons      xmin     ymin      xmax     ymax
          0     0      108 -84.32385 33.88199 -75.45698 36.58965

``` r
head(nc$attributes[, c("AREA", "PERIMETER", "NAME", "FIPS")])
```

       AREA PERIMETER        NAME  FIPS
    1 0.114     1.442        Ashe 37009
    2 0.061     1.231   Alleghany 37005
    3 0.143     1.630       Surry 37171
    4 0.070     2.968   Currituck 37053
    5 0.153     2.206 Northampton 37131

The geometry is TDA’s, so TDA’s plotting draws it.

Some of these commands compare one object type against another in the
same structure. A set of polygons on its own has no lines or points for
them to find, and saying so is the right answer rather than an error.

## TDA’s help

The program carries its help text for every command, and
[`tda_help()`](https://janmarvin.github.io/TDA/reference/tda_help.md)
reads it. This is the fastest way to find what a command’s options are
actually called, since the R wrappers deliberately do not expose all of
them by name.

Box 12tda_help

``` r
cat(head(tda_help("ploth"), 20), sep = "\n")
```

    ploth: The ploth command can be used to plot a histogram. Syntax is:

        ploth(
            x=...,      intervals, required
            w=...,      variable for weights
            dscal=...,  scaling factor, def. 1.0
            s=...,      s=0 (default) classes are left closed
                        s=1 classes are left open
            ns=...,     ns=1, don't plot vertical lines, def. ns=0
            lt=...,     line type, def. 1 (solid line)
            lw=...,     line width, def. 0.2 (mm)
            gs=...,     grey scale value, def. 1 (white)
            nc=...,     nc=1 if no clipping, def. 0
            df=...,     print table to output file
            fmt=...,    print format for output file, def. 10.4
        ) = variable;

        There must be exactly one variable name on the right-hand side. Also
        one has to use the x parameter to specify a set of intervals (classes)
        for the histogram. The syntax is

            x=x1,x2,...,xn,   or   x=x1(d)x2,

        x1 must be not greater than the minimum of the values of the variable,
        and xn must not smaller than the maximum of the values of the variable.
        The command requires a valid setup for plots and uses the currently
        defined coordinate system. The heights of the histogram are calculated
        in such a way that the areas equal the frequencies. A corresponding
        frequency table can be requested with the df parameter. The output file
        will then contain n - 1 lines with the following entries:

        1) begin of class
        2) end of class
        3) absolute frequency
        4) relative frequency
        5) height of histogram

    See also: atab
    ploth: The ploth command can be used to plot a histogram. Syntax is:

        ploth(
            x=...,      intervals, required
            w=...,      variable for weights
            dscal=...,  scaling factor, def. 1.0
            s=...,      s=0 (default) classes are left closed
                        s=1 classes are left open

## Running TDA directly

[`tda_run()`](https://janmarvin.github.io/TDA/reference/tda_run.md)
takes command-file text and runs it, which is the escape hatch for
anything without a wrapper.
[`tda_block()`](https://janmarvin.github.io/TDA/reference/tda_write_data.md)
builds one command from named arguments so the syntax does not have to
be written by hand.

Box 13A command file, from R

``` r
d <- data.frame(X = c(1, 2, 3, 4), Y = c(2, 4, 6, 9))
res <- tda_run(c(tda_nvar(d), "dstat;"), data = d)
cat(grep("^ *(Variable|X|Y)", res$output, value = TRUE), sep = "\n")
```

    Variable    Minimum    Maximum       Mean   Std.Dev.    Sum of values
    X            1.0000     4.0000     2.5000     1.2910          10.0000
    Y            2.0000     9.0000     5.2500     2.9861          21.0000

Every wrapper returns its `$run`, so the command file a call generated
can always be read back. This is worth knowing when a result looks
wrong: the question is usually what TDA was asked, not what it computed.

Box 14What a wrapper actually sent

``` r
fit <- tda_lsreg(Y ~ X, d)
cat(fit$run$commands, sep = "\n")
```

    rdataframe;
    lsreg(mfmt=24.16, tfmt=24.16) = Y,X;

## The expression language

TDA’s operators are available without a data set through
[`tda_evalf()`](https://janmarvin.github.io/TDA/reference/tda_integrate.md),
and its distribution functions are the ones the manual lists in 5.2.5 –
`nd`, `ndf`, `td`, `chd`, `fd`, `mr`, `poisson`, `negbin`. They agree
with R’s, which is checked by a differential fuzzer on every run of the
test suite, so either side gives the same numbers.

Box 15The same quantity, twice

``` r
sprintf("%.17g", c(tda_evalf("nd(x)", options = list(x = 1.96))$value,
                   pnorm(1.96)))
```

    [1] "0.97500210485082472" "0.97500210485177963"

``` r
sprintf("%.17g", c(tda_evalf("mr(x)", options = list(x = 0.5))$value,
                   dnorm(0.5) / (1 - pnorm(0.5))))
```

    [1] "1.141077770368061"  "1.1410777703680643"

## Character data

TDA holds fixed-width string variables, and a character or factor column
reaches it:
[`tda_nvar()`](https://janmarvin.github.io/TDA/reference/tda_write_data.md)
declares it as `str(n,m)` and
[`tda_strings()`](https://janmarvin.github.io/TDA/reference/tda_strings.md)
brings it back. The four string operators – `strlen`, `strsp`, `strv`,
`strvp` – work on it.

Box 16Strings through TDA

``` r
d2 <- data.frame(ID = 1:3, Name = c("Ashe", "Alleghany", "Surry"),
                 Area = c(0.114, 0.061, 0.143))
res <- tda_run(c(tda_nvar(d2), "pdata() = out.txt;"), data = d2)
tda_strings(res)
```

    $Name
    [1] "Ashe"      "Alleghany" "Surry"    

## Graphs

Chapter 7 of the manual covers relational data, and the 31 `tda_g_*`
commands implement it: components, cliques, cut points, spanning trees,
cycles, flows, shortest paths, and the social-network measures of 7.6.
They are documented but easy to miss, so one example, on a small graph.

Box 17A graph, and some of what TDA asks of it

``` r
e <- data.frame(from = c(1, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 5),
                to   = c(2, 3, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7))
g <- tda_graph(e, directed = FALSE)
tda_g_degrees(g)
```

      index node in_degree out_degree loops degree
    1     1    1         2          2     0      2
    2     2    2         2          2     0      2
    3     3    3         3          3     0      3
    4     4    4         2          2     0      2
    5     5    5         3          3     0      3
    6     6    6         1          1     0      1
    7     7    7         1          1     0      1

``` r
tda_g_components(g)
```

    Call: tda_g_components(g)

    Cases: 7 

     component n i node_i
             1 7 1      1
             1 7 2      2
             1 7 3      3
             1 7 4      4
             1 7 5      5
             1 7 6      6
             1 7 7      7

``` r
tda_g_cutpoints(g)
```

    Call: tda_g_cutpoints(g)

    Cases: 7 

     V1 V2 V3 V4 V5 V6
      1  7  3  3  4  5
